issues: claim cites unknown ids ['10.1016/heliyon.2024.e32220']: Adoption of generative AI is driven primarily by habit forma

llm_major: RQ1 (direct effects on research productivity: output volume, completion time, efficiency metrics) is answered only by one survey of UK academics (10.1007/s42438-023-00440-6) reporting perceived workload relief, not objective productivity measures for graduate students, making the sub-question effectively unanswered despite passing the count threshold.

RQ2 (research quality and rigor outcomes in graduate research) cites hallucination studies (10.2196/53164) and AI article generation experiments (10.2196/47049) but lacks evidence from actual graduate dissertations or theses; the single coding study (10.3390/app14104115) is undergraduate programming only, leaving graduate-specific quality effects unmeasured.

RQ3 (mechanisms: cognitive load, skill development, problem-solving) relies heavily on undergraduate samples and non-research contexts (digital storytelling, programming education); only 10.3390/app14104115 (n=32 undergraduates, 10-week duration) directly links AI reliance to academic performance, providing insufficient evidence of mechanisms in graduate research workflows.
llm_minor: The conflict between workflow compatibility (10.1145/3652154: software engineers) and perceived usefulness (10.1007/s10755-023-09686-1, 10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e32220: university students) as adoption drivers is explained by population and task differences, but this hypothesis is not empirically tested in graduate populations.

RQ5 (academic integrity, plagiarism, dependence) is addressed through reviews, commentaries, and one hallucination rate study (10.2196/53164), but no empirical studies measure actual rates of integrity violations or plagiarism among graduate students as a function of AI use.

RQ6 (best practices and training) is synthesized from policy analyses (10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100348) and expert commentary (10.1080/0144929x.2024.2394886) rather than experimental tests; no randomized trials of training interventions exist to support specific recommendations for graduate research workflows.
actions: search rq2: longitudinal assessments of graduate dissertation or thesis chapter quality (using blind expert rubrics) correlated with AI use intensity over study duration; or comparative analysis of quality metrics (originality, rigor, literature integration) in dissertations submitted by high versus low AI users

search rq3: experimental or longitudinal studies of graduate students measuring cognitive load (via validated scales or task performance metrics), skill atrophy/development, or problem-solving approach changes as a function of AI tool use intensity during dissertation research

For RQ3, new queries emphasize validated cognitive load measurement, skill trajectories, and problem-solving changes in dissertation contexts, not undergraduate digital storytelling or programming education.

llm_major: RQ1 on direct productivity effects relies entirely on one survey of UK academics (10.1007/s42438-023-00440-6) reporting perceived workload relief, not objective graduate student output metrics; no randomized trials or longitudinal studies measuring actual dissertation progress, pages drafted, or completion time exist, leaving this sub-question effectively unanswered despite passing count thresholds.

RQ2 on research quality and rigor in graduate research relies on hallucination rates from isolated tasks (reference generation in systematic reviews, legal research tools) and expert review of 4 AI-generated articles, but provides zero evidence of quality assessment in actual graduate dissertations or theses; the single undergraduate study linking tool reliance to performance (10.3390/app14104115, n=32, 10 weeks, programming only) does not generalize to graduate research contexts.

The conflict between performance improvement (10.1287/orsc.2023.18430, 10.1186/s41239-025-00526-0) and performance decline (10.3390/app14104115) is presented with a hypothesis but without sufficient evidence to distinguish when each pathway occurs in graduate research specifically; mechanisms operate in undergraduate programming (10 weeks), business problem-solving (crowdsourcing), and digital storytelling contexts, not graduate dissertation workflows.

RQ5 on academic integrity violations relies on hallucination rates and policy reviews rather than empirical audits of actual plagiarism, citation inaccuracies, or undetected violations in graduate student work; no measurement of integrity violation prevalence or correlation with AI use intensity exists among graduate students.
llm_minor: The conditional statement on gender and disciplinary differences (10.1007/s10755-024-09774-w) identifies that male STEM students differ from female non-STEM students in adoption patterns, but the study was conducted at a single U.S. institution in Fall 2023 and provides no explicit causal mechanism linking field-specific epistemologies or prior technical experience to AI integration outcomes.

Gap 5 proposes testing training interventions for graduate students, but the current evidence base includes only policy reviews and expert commentary; no pilot studies or early-stage evidence on intervention feasibility, preferred training modality, or effect size benchmarks exist to guide the proposed RCT design.
